newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS -- Fed officials content with status quo.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -- Fed officials content with status quo.

text.p: Two Federal Reserve officials this weekend signaled comfort with the state of the U.S. economy and suggested they were content with steady interest rates for now.
"What's not to like?" Fed Governor Laurence Meyer retorted when queried about the high level of consumer confidence.
Speaking Sunday with reporters at an American Economic Association conference, Meyer described inflation as "low" and "stable" and noted that unemployment was also low.
He said the risks in the economy seemed evenly balanced to the upside and downside, although there is always the danger that those risks could shift in either direction.
"While there might be some danger in the forecast, that's enough to keep us alert but not enough to take us off the sidelines right now," Meyer said.
Looking ahead to 1997, Meyer predicted trend growth at a rate of 2 to 2.5 percent.

His colleague, Governor Lawrence Lindsey, who also spoke with reporters at the conference, was less specific about his economic outlook but said the most likely scenario was moderate growth with continued tame inflation.
Like Meyer, Lindsey had few complaints about the current climate. "It's hard to quarrel with 2-1/2 to three percent inflation (and) 5-1/4 percent unemployment," he said. "It looks pretty good to me."

After a spurt of growth earlier in the year, gross domestic product grew by 2.1 percent in the third quarter of 1996 -- a pace considered by many at the Fed to be right in line with sustainable, non-inflationary growth.
The government does not yet have an official tally for fourth-quarter growth, but many economists are predicting a similarly moderate pace.
Still, some analysts see hints of a possible pickup in growth that could push unemployment down further and raise the risks of wage-driven inflation.

After a jump in the National Association of Purchasing Management's manufacturing index and reports depicting continued strength in the housing market, some bond traders have been fretting about the potential for an interest rate hike should the economy appear set to overheat.
Neither Meyer nor Lindsey gave any indication of alarm.

Stressing that the Fed is always vigilant about inflation, Meyer acknowledged the low unemployment rate could pose a risk if the economy gathers steam. On the other hand, inflation has behaved well recently, he said. "Right now, we are looking at measures of core inflation that are still declining."
For his part, Lindsey said all the evidence suggests that inflation should remain tame.
Although they responded to reporters' questions about short-run economic developments, both Meyer and Lindsey focused on longer-term issues in their formal presentations to the conference here.
Meyer, who sat on a panel looking at ways policymakers use economic models, said the Fed board was interested in exploring the usefulness of monetary policy rules for the setting of interest rates.
In particular, he highlighted rules such as one developed by Stanford University economist John Taylor that bases interest-rate determinations on developments with growth and inflation.
Dubbing such rules as "monetarism without money," Meyer said they can help provide discipline to the policy process but they can't take the place of human judgment.
Appearing at a separate panel discussion about monetary policy, inflation and economic stability, Lindsey expressed reservations about using rules to govern policy.
"I think that people can do better than a rule," Lindsey said, listing greater flexibility and accountability as some of the benefits of relying on individual discretion as opposed to rules.
